newsitem.title: POLAND: Rain on Central Europe raises new flood fears.
newsitem.headline: Rain on Central Europe raises new flood fears.

text.p: Rains fell for a third day on Poland and the Czech Republic, raising river levels dangerously high on Sunday in regions which had yet to recover from earlier floods that killed nearly 100 people.

Poland's central crisis committee said there was little chance that the cataclysm of the past two weeks would be repeated, as the rain was not as heavy as first feared and endangered communities were better prepared than they were the last time.

"For the time being it is bad, but there is no tragedy as far as rainfall is concerned," committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes told Reuters. "The lesson from the previous phase is that all are working to prevent another tragedy," he added.
In Austria, shipping on the river Danube, which flows from the Alps to the Black Sea, was suspended along a 90 km (50 mile) stretch between Linz and Krems, Austrian state television reported.

Elsewhere in Austria, flood waters retreated as clouds parted but emergency services remained on alert, with more showers forecast for Monday. The northern province of Upper Austria and the Danube basin have so far been worst hit by Austria's worst floods this century.
For hundreds of thousands of Poles, reeling from floods over the past two weeks, the overall picture gave cold comfort as many returned to heaving sandbags to reinforce dykes.
Urgent preparations were under way in Jelenia Gora and around the Silesian towns of Raciborz and Legnica, where streets in the outskirts were already flooded on Sunday.
The Polish floods this month killed at least 49 people, inundated a thousand towns and villages and swamped half a million hectares (1.25 million acres) of land in the south and west.
In Klodzko on the Czech border, residents who had already lost homes, businesses and farms, watched the rain with dread.
"We're scared of this constant rain because it could mean the water will reach us again," said small-holder Krystyna Sobanska, whose uninsured crops were ruined and house is in danger of collapse.
"The water has robbed me of everything, two pigs, two cows, the chickens...everything we built up all our lives, including our farm machinery is gone," she told a Reuters reporter.
Over the frontier in the suffering Czech Republic, there were thousands of similar tragedies.
Heavy rain in the mountainous Czech northeast again turned rivers into raging torrents, while several districts were on the highest flood alert and hundreds of people were evacuated.
Alerts were declared on rivers including the Morava and the Odra, which flooded both Czech and Polish communities last week.

Czech authorities had warned on Thursday of a possible new wave of floods following the first, which was triggered by days of torrential rain two weeks ago and devastated vast areas of the eastern third of the country, killing at least 45 people.

The floods in both countries have cut road, rail and telecommunications links and inundated valuable industrial and crop land, causing economic disruption which is only just beginning to be estimated.
In Poland, officials are talking about losses of billions of zlotys.
The Polish government, accused by the opposition of doing too little too late, was flinging resources and personnel, including around 45,000 troops and 80 helicopters, into relief and rescue efforts.
A special government body set up to combat the effects of the disaster promised to have a draft plan ready by Tuesday.

Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Saturday that unless something very unexpected happened he would not declare a state of emergency in affected areas. Such an announcement would automatically delay parliamentary elections due on September 21.
The rains also put pressure on dykes in eastern Germany, where officials feared they may not stand the strain. Police closed off bridges over the Odra to Poland and evacuated small numbers of people.
